style: Say casually and naturally, like a friendly teenager explaining something
lines: Pick something from the tray, then drag in space to throw it. A longer drag throws it faster.
Crash. Drag the time bar back to undo it, then throw again.
That one got away. It was too fast for the star to pull it back.
Tap a planet, then tap Follow. Now your throws aim around it, so you can give it a moon.
Tap Goals to see your stickers and what to try next.
This is our real solar system, on the first day of 2000. Tap x16 to watch the outer planets move.
Drag in space to add a comet. Tap a planet, then Follow to watch from its view.
Tap Earth, then tap Follow. Watch Mars from Earth for a few years.
Tap True size to see how small the planets really are.
Two suns. Throw a planet around both of them, far out.
Three stars share one figure eight. Tap a dancer, then tap Faster once.
This moon keeps crashing. Drag the time bar to the start, tap the moon, then tap Slower a few times.
A giant in a dust disk. Watch its path.
A whirl around a black hole. Drag Gravity down to 0.4 and watch.
Space is full. Crash some together, or pick one and tap Remove.
Gone. It flew too far to follow.
Saved on this device.
Let go to throw. The dashed line shows where it will go.
Drag from it to throw it again, or use Faster, Slower and Turn.
Throw or change something to start a new timeline, or tap Play.

An orbit is falling and missing: it falls toward the star the whole time, but moves sideways fast enough to miss.
The masses add up, and the new body keeps going with the push of both.
From any spot, escape speed is about 1.41 times the speed for a circle.
With no pull, a moving thing goes straight at a steady speed. Gravity is what bends the path.
Closer orbits are shorter and faster. Mercury takes 88 days; Neptune takes 165 years.
On a stretched orbit, a body races past the star and crawls far away. Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years.
More mass, more pull: the neighbors' orbits tighten. Big stars burn hotter and bluer.
A planet tugs its star around in a small circle. Astronomers find planets around other stars by that wobble.
A moon stays only close to its planet. Farther out, the star's pull carries it away.
Moons that go backwards stay steady farther out. Neptune's big moon Triton goes backwards.
A lighter star can let a planet go. Less mass means a weaker pull; a small speed change can decide whether it escapes.
A ring is countless tiny moons. Inner bits move faster, so a clump smears into a circle. Saturn's rings are ice.
Two stars circle a point between them, their center of mass. Nearly half of Sun-like stars have a partner.
A close pass behind a moving planet borrows some of its speed. Voyager 2 did this at Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus.
Which pull wins can change in a close pass, so moons can be lost and caught.
Sixty degrees ahead of or behind a planet, the pulls balance. Jupiter has thousands of Trojan asteroids there.
A planet can circle two suns if it stays far out, a bit more than twice their spacing. Kepler-16b is one.
A slower moon stayed closer and safer. A small change now is a big change later.
A big planet sweeps its path clear. Clearing its lane is part of being a planet; Pluto has not cleared its lane.
Far away, a black hole pulls just like a star of the same mass. It only swallows what comes very close.
Three equal stars can share one figure-eight path, found in 1993. Small nudges keep it going; big ones break it.
Earth passes Mars on the inside track, so Mars seems to back up for a while about every 26 months.
Seen from Earth, Venus draws five loops in eight years: 13 Venus years almost equal 8 Earth years.
Voyager 2 flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune in 12 years.
